So who's going to walk through the discv5 protocol to ensure that a multiaddr is sufficient to enter into the protocol with another node? So I think in part the difficulty comes in the following scenario. Consider Node A has an unsigned ENR or multiaddr of node B and tries to connect. A -> Random -> B B -> WhoAreYou -> A A -> AuthMessage + LocalENR -> B (B has A's ENR, A still only has multi addr and session is established) A -> Packets -> B A still doesn't have an ENR and shouldn't add B to routing table. If ENR seq start at 0. During a PING A needs to say which seq no it has for B, but it has none. If it says 0, B may not reply right. It could guess a number. We then have sessions established some of which potentially we dont know ENR's of peers. shouldn't B's ENR be made mandatory then? A -> Packets -> B, (B -> ENR -> A, [B -> Packets -> A]*), else disconnect If A is required to have an ENR to connect to B then we dont (if we want to connect via multiaddr, we would need some way to retrieve the ENR as you suggest) The wire protocol doesn't forbid using a mulitaddr/enode, although I tried something similar previously but it didnt work. Like you guys have mentioned though it would be odd to have only 2 peers perform a succesful handshake but only 1 peer has the other's ENR I understand the issue now ENR seq 0 is special If you want a node's ENR, just send FINDNODE(0) This is something you can add in your implementation to resolve this issue: if your local reference to the node is an 'unsigned' ENR you created from the multiaddr, just request the remote ENR after handshake and you'll have the real one. In WHOAREYOU, sequence number zero means the same as 'I don't have your ENR' Sure. This seems do-able. In the rust impl sending messages and establishing sessions require the node's ENR. In principle this could be relaxed to ip/port/key. Does go currently require ENR's to send messages? Kind of. The Go abstraction for ENR goes like this: We have a package p2p/enr for the ENR format We have another package, p2p/enode, which has a representation of a 'validated' ENR, enode.Node But we also have other ways of creating enode.Node, i.e. from public key + IP + ports Most code that works with nodes doesn't really care if it came from a signed ENR or not, but the code that does can find out by checking for it. For example, I can insert unsigned nodes into the Kademlia table, I just need to take care to filter them out when responding to discv5 FINDNODE Oh right. What would be the point of an unsigned node in the table? It can happen if you insert it locally, because it was passed on the command line I've built it so the rust type system wont allow it. And there's no such thing as an Unsigned ENR.. only invalid binary junk :p yeah, we reject it straight up Like in the case we discussed, I mean. I'm pretty sure there is no issue with it in go Ok cool. Well. I can at least see a solution here, just takes a bit more engineering Ultimately it depends on what you want for users Afri didn't like working with ENRs because they are super opaque Yeah, I like ENR's but I can see the frustration they can cause I originally considered defining a readable text encoding for ENR, but didn't do it because you can't modify them and still keep them valid, and also because most K/V pairs will just be binary data. That's why I went with the lazy base64 option Yeah. Fair call. I half-implemented ed25519. Its good to hear its on the radar. It would be nice for us if the NodeId matched the PeerId.. i.e we use a multihash. I think we actually just use the pubkey (there's no hashing). Yeah, I'll look into it. I was thinking we could just go with sha256 of the key I think it won't matter. Because we can convert a PeerId to the public key and hence a NodeId whatever the function. The hash needs to be in there because ID distribution must be uniform, and public keys usually don't have uniform random distribution oh yeah, good point But maybe ed25519 keys are, ol' Bernstein might've thought of that Will check next week ahaha 🤞 I'm off. excerpts.author: agemanning
excerpts.content:
So I think in part the difficulty comes in the following scenario. Consider Node A has an unsigned ENR or multiaddr of node B and tries to connect. 
A -> Random -> B
B -> WhoAreYou -> A
A -> AuthMessage + LocalENR -> B (B has A's ENR, A still only has multi addr and session is established) 
A -> Packets -> B
A still doesn't have an ENR and shouldn't add B to routing table. If ENR seq start at 0. During a PING A needs to say which seq no it has for B, but it has none. If it says 0, B may not reply right. It could guess a number. 
We then have sessions established some of which potentially we dont know ENR's of peers.
